lines.text: At 3:14 and 7 seconds, every clock on Earth skipped the same second.
Phones. Train stations. Wristwatches. All of them.
The atomic clocks in Colorado, Paris and Tokyo confirmed it.
Exactly one second was gone. Not lost. Removed.
Every government asked the same question. Where did it go?
But the strangest part wasn't the missing second.
It was that the cameras kept recording through it.
Twenty-four frames from a second that never happened.
Engineers checked the footage for tampering. There was none.
And in every camera on Earth, the same man was standing there.
On a subway platform in Tokyo. In a market in Lagos. On a farm in Iowa.
Always with his back to the lens.
Thousands of cameras. Thousands of cities. The same man. The same suit.
Frame by frame, he was closer to the camera.
And in the last frame, he had started to turn around.
Nobody has seen his face. The footage always ends one frame too soon.
Then historians found him in older records.
A monk in 1582 wrote that an hour went missing, and a man stood in every doorway.
A cave painting in France shows a tall figure, turned away from the hunters.
A photograph from 1888. A film reel from 1961.
Every time time skipped, he was one step closer.
Someone counted the steps.
There is one left.
When he takes it, he will be facing us.
The footage was deleted within a week.
Quietly, cameras around the world were turned to face the walls.
Observatories stopped publishing their clock data.
In 2022, the world voted to stop adding leap seconds.
Nobody explained why.
Some people still won't look at a clock at 3:14.
Some people say that at night they hear a single tick that doesn't belong to any clock.
When he finally turns around, whose face will he have?
